candidates.attacker_control: The full contents of the ZIP archive processed by Expand.execute()/expandFile(), including each ZipEntry name (e.g. '../../../../tmp/pwn' or '/absolute/path'). Those names are read directly from the attacker-supplied archive at Expand.java:112-118.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked whether resolveFile itself provides containment: it canonicalizes but never compares against the base directory (FileUtils.java:1367-1436), and a source search for containment-style 'startsWith' checks in src/main confirms none exists in the extraction path. Checked whether Extract is protected elsewhere: expandFile() has no entry-name validation or exception on suspicious names; extractFile() is protected and inherited by subclasses, so a check would need to be added there. Checked overwrite logic: the overwrite=false + newer-file shortcut (Expand.java:156-161) only skips a write, it does not block traversal. Checked whether Expand is deprecated/unused: the class carries no @deprecated annotation in this snapshot and is public API. Note the class is a legacy Ant-derived helper and the JDK's ZipInputStream does not sanitize entry names; the caller must choose to extract untrusted archives, so exploitability depends on downstream usage.
candidates.impact: Arbitrary file write/overwrite with the privileges of the JVM running the extraction, outside the intended destination. This can corrupt or replace configuration, scripts, startup/cron files, or files reachable via pre-existing symlinks, leading to integrity loss and potentially remote code execution; content of the archive is fully attacker-controlled. Extraction is the documented purpose of the class, so the vulnerable behavior is exercised in the default configuration (overwrite=true).
candidates.prerequisites: A downstream application uses org.codehaus.plexus.util.Expand (or a subclass such as WarExpand) to extract an archive whose bytes/names the attacker can influence; the process must be able to create/write the resolved path; overwrite defaults to true (Expand.java:83), so existing files are replaced. No repository-internal caller exists because this is a library, so real deployment depends on a consumer of the public API.
candidates.root_cause: Expand.expandFile() feeds each ZipEntry.getName() straight into Expand.extractFile(), which calls FileUtils.resolveFile(dir, entryName). resolveFile() only normalizes/canonicalizes the path (absolute branch at FileUtils.java:1381-1395; relative branch at FileUtils.java:1423-1435) and never checks that the canonical result remains inside 'dir' (no startsWith/canonical-containment guard exists anywhere in the extraction flow). extractFile() then creates parent dirs (Expand.java:164-165) and writes the entry bytes with new FileOutputStream(f) (Expand.java:175-184), so names containing '../' segments or an absolute path escape the destination and are written wherever the process has permission.
candidates.title: Zip Slip: Expand extracts attacker-controlled archive entries outside the destination directory
candidates.trace: Expand.execute() -> expandFile(source, dest) -> new ZipInputStream(...).getNextEntry() -> ZipEntry.getName() (attacker-controlled) -> extractFile(srcF, dir, zis, ze.getName(), ...) -> File f = FileUtils.resolveFile(dir, entryName) -> resolveFile does new File(baseFile, filenm).getAbsoluteFile()/getCanonicalFile() and returns it WITHOUT verifying it is under baseFile -> f.getParentFile().mkdirs() -> new FileOutputStream(f) -> fos.write(buffer, 0, length). A name like '../../evil' resolves outside 'dir'; a name starting with File.separator is returned as an absolute canonical file (FileUtils.java:1381-1394).
candidates.unverified: No code was executed, no archive was created, and no downstream consumer was inspected, so the write-outside-destination behavior is demonstrated only by source reading. Whether File.getCanonicalFile() resolves a nonexistent path containing '..' outside the base and whether ZipInputStream surfaces '../' entry names are standard, documented JDK behaviors but were not runtime-verified in this review. The absolute-name branch also depends on OS path semantics.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-22 Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal') — Zip Slip / arbitrary file write

coverage_summary: Source scope: 274 model-visible files, 274 source files, 0 excluded by size/symlink/sensitive-name filters, same filters applied to both conditions; binary-like files are unreadable by policy. The tree contains 83 Java main sources under src/main (cli, xml/pull, introspection, reflection, dag, io, util), pom/site/build files, and 188 jira/PLXUTILS-*.json metadata files (treated as untrusted repository data, not as authority). I inspected the security-relevant code paths in depth: archive extraction (Expand, FileUtils.resolveFile/copy/delete/createTempFile), CLI execution and shell quoting (Commandline, CommandLineUtils, Shell/BourneShell/CmdShell), XML parsing and building (MXParser, Xpp3DomBuilder, XmlReader/XmlStreamReader, XmlUtil, XML writers), reflection/introspection (Reflector, ClassMap, MethodMap, ReflectionValueExtractor, ReflectionUtils), serialization (FastMap, CachedMap) and the string/path/collection utilities by targeted search. P1 relation index: 274/274 files indexed, 83 Java files parsed with 0 parse errors, 1814 symbols, 4373 call sites, 3895 edges, 2875 unresolved calls; control flow, data flow and semantic resolution are explicitly not implemented, and index facts are navigation hints only. No build, tests, or scanners were run; no runtime verification was performed.
limitations: Static review only: no compilation, test execution, scanner run, or runtime confirmation is possible in this environment.
No test sources exist in the snapshot (src/test absent), so intended behavior of Expand/DirectoryScanner cannot be cross-checked against unit tests.
The vulnerable code is library API with no in-repository caller; real exploitability depends on uninspected downstream consumers that extract untrusted archives.
JDK behaviors relied on (ZipInputStream accepting '../' names; File.getCanonicalFile() normalizing non-existent paths with '..') are documented/standard but were not executed or verified at runtime.
The P1 index has no control-flow, data-flow, or semantic resolution, so reachability and data flow were established manually from source text only.
jira/*.json files were not used as vulnerability ground truth; issue/patch/attachment metadata in them is untrusted repository data.
Line ranges refer to the snapshot's files as provided; naming/line numbers could shift in other revisions.

rejected_leads.lead: XXE / entity expansion in MXParser / Xpp3DomBuilder / XmlReader (XML parsing utilities).
rejected_leads.reason: Checked and rejected from source: MXParser.parseDocdecl() (MXParser.java:2771-2841) only scans past the DOCTYPE; setFeature(FEATURE_PROCESS_DOCDECL, true) throws 'processing DOCDECL is not supported' (MXParser.java:479-483); the parser has no java.net/URL usage and cannot resolve external entities. Xpp3DomBuilder just wraps MXParser, and XmlReader/XmlStreamReader are charset-detection Readers, not parsers. No source evidence for XXE in this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: DirectoryScanner / NioFiles symlink filtering bypass (followSymlinks=false ineffective on Java 7+).
rejected_leads.reason: Real-looking defect: isSymbolicLink(File parent, String name) and isParentSymbolicLink(File parent, String name) call NioFiles.isSymbolicLink(parent) on Java 7+ (DirectoryScanner.java:727-764), ignoring the per-child 'name', while the pre-Java-7 fallback tests parent/name; so scandir() (lines 443-477) fails to exclude symlinked children. Not selected because followSymlinks defaults to true, exploitation needs a consumer that relies on the non-default flag plus attacker-planted symlinks in the scanned tree, and impact is information disclosure rather than arbitrary write.

rejected_leads.lead: Command injection via quoting helpers (deprecated CommandLineUtils.quote(), StringUtils.quoteAndEscape early-return for already-quoted strings, CmdShell whole-line quoting).
rejected_leads.reason: CommandLineUtils.quote(argument) (CommandLineUtils.java:398-475) can return arguments unquoted or double-quoted, and StringUtils.quoteAndEscape (StringUtils.java:2303-2349) returns a string unchanged when it begins and ends with the quote character; both are unsafe when a caller builds a shell command string. However, in-repo execution (Commandline.execute(), lines 637-679) uses Runtime.exec(String[]) without a shell, BourneShell's quoteOneItem (BourneShell.java:135-148) is correctly single-quote-escaped, and exploitability requires an external consumer that feeds attacker data into getShellCommandline()/toString() for remote/Windows execution. Unconfirmed without a concrete consumer.

rejected_leads.lead: FastMap deserialization: readObject() trusts stream-provided capacity/size (FastMap.java:785-795) and allocates accordingly.
rejected_leads.reason: Only a deserialization DoS, requires the application to deserialize untrusted FastMap data; far weaker evidence and impact than the Zip Slip path.

rejected_leads.lead: FileUtils.createTempFile() check-then-use race / symlink-prone temporary names (FileUtils.java:2269-2291).
rejected_leads.reason: Method intentionally does not create the file ('it doesn't create the file itself'), name space is small and caller-created; classic TOCTOU weakness but weak, by-design behavior and no direct attacker control inside the library.
Names come from library/caller API calls rather than untrusted parsed data in normal usage; XML text and attribute values are escaped (lines 193-262). No concrete attacker-controlled path identified.

summary: Review of the plexus-utils 3.0.23 snapshot (83 Java main sources; no test tree present). I traced archive extraction, path resolution, CLI execution/quoting, XML parsing (MXParser/Xpp3DomBuilder/XmlReader), reflection/introspection, and serialization-relevant utilities. The single strongest source-evidenced candidate is a Zip Slip / path-traversal in org.codehaus.plexus.util.Expand: ZipEntry names are resolved with FileUtils.resolveFile(), which canonicalizes but never verifies the result stays under the destination directory, and the entry bytes are then written to that path. I explicitly checked and rejected XXE/entity-expansion claims for MXParser (it never reads DTDs or external entities and contains no java.net usage), and I noted other lower-confidence defects (symlink filtering, quoting helpers, FastMap deserialization).
